# Points, Vectors, and Directions

The same coordinate column can play two different geometric roles

- [Why distinguish points from vectors?](#why-distinguish-points-from-vectors)
- [The operations reveal the roles](#the-operations-reveal-the-roles)
- [Choosing an origin hides the distinction](#choosing-an-origin-hides-the-distinction)
- [Lines and planes combine points with directions](#lines-and-planes-combine-points-with-directions)

## Why distinguish points from vectors? {#why-distinguish-points-from-vectors}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
### Point

- a [location]{.alert}
- written $P,Q,\ldots$
- with chosen coordinates $P=(p_1,p_2,\ldots)$
- has no intrinsic direction or length
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
### Vector

- a [displacement or direction]{.alert}
- written $\vct{u},\vct{v},\ldots$
- from origin $O$, $\vct{p}=\overrightarrow{OP}=[p_1,p_2,\ldots]^{\mathsf T}$
- has length and direction; translation leaves it unchanged
:::
:::

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=Q-P
$$

::: {.key-point}
Points say where; vectors say how to move
:::

::: {.notes}
Teaching purpose: coordinate notation makes points and vectors look identical,
so students may miss why homogeneous solution sets are vector spaces while
nonhomogeneous solution sets usually are not. Use the physical language first:
a point is where you are, a vector tells you how to move, and the difference
between two possible locations is a displacement. Then preview the algebraic
payoff: differences between solutions of $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ solve the
homogeneous system.
The coordinate notation is an example after choosing an origin and axes;
parentheses versus column brackets are not what makes an object a point or a
vector.
:::

## The operations reveal the roles {#the-operations-reveal-the-roles}

| Operation | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| $Q-P$ | vector | displacement from $P$ to $Q$ |
| $P+\vct{v}$ | point | move from $P$ by $\vct{v}$ |
| $\vct{u}+\vct{v}$ | vector | combine displacements |
| $c\vct{v}$ | vector | scale or reverse a displacement |
| $P+Q$ | — | no origin-independent geometric meaning |

$a\vct{u}+b\vct{v}$ — a [linear combination]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#given-output-solve-column-weights), with scalar weights $a,b$

The expression

$$
(1-t)P+tQ=P+t(Q-P)
$$

does have geometric meaning because its coefficients sum to $1$

## Choosing an origin hides the distinction {#choosing-an-origin-hides-the-distinction}

After choosing an origin $O$ and axes in $\reals^3$:

$$
P=(p_1,p_2,p_3)
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\vct{p}=\overrightarrow{OP}
=\begin{bmatrix}p_1\\p_2\\p_3\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here $P,Q$ are [points]{.alert}; $\vct{p},\vct{q}$ are their position vectors;
$\vct{u},\vct{v}$ are directions. Other symbols can play the same roles

Moving the origin changes $\vct{p}$ and $\vct{q}$, but not the displacement

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vct{q}-\vct{p}
$$

Parentheses versus column brackets do not determine the role; the geometry does

::: {.notes}
The tuple and column forms help display the distinction in this deck; their
shapes alone do not determine whether an object is a point or a vector.
The role and the chosen origin determine the meaning. The same construction
works in $\reals^n$ with $n$ coordinates.
:::

## Lines and planes combine points with directions {#lines-and-planes-combine-points-with-directions}

A line needs one point and one nonzero direction:

$$
L=\{P+t\vct{v}:t\in\reals\}
$$

A plane needs one point and two independent directions:

$$
\Pi=\{P+s\vct{u}+t\vct{v}:s,t\in\reals\}
$$

$s\vct{u}+t\vct{v}$ — a [linear combination]{.alert} of the direction vectors

Changing the point on the same line or plane does not change its directions

Only when the set passes through the origin can its points also be treated as
a collection of vectors closed under addition and scaling

::: {.key-point}
Point $+$ directions describes a translated, or [affine]{.alert}, set
:::

# Solution Sets Have Directions

This is why the point–vector distinction matters in linear algebra

- [Homogeneous systems produce directions](#homogeneous-systems-produce-directions)
- [Nonhomogeneous systems translate those directions](#nonhomogeneous-systems-translate-those-directions)
- [Free variables count the directions](#free-variables-count-the-directions)
- [Read the affine structure from elimination](#read-the-affine-structure-from-elimination)

## Homogeneous systems produce directions {#homogeneous-systems-produce-directions}

The solutions of

$$
\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}
$$

include $\vct{0}$ and are [closed under linear combinations]{.alert}:
every linear combination of homogeneous solutions is another homogeneous solution

$$
\mat{A}\vct{z}_1=\vct{0},
\quad
\mat{A}\vct{z}_2=\vct{0}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mat{A}(c_1\vct{z}_1+c_2\vct{z}_2)=\vct{0}
$$

These solutions are [directions]{.alert} that the matrix cannot detect:

$$
\mat{A}(\vct{x}+\vct{z})=\mat{A}\vct{x}
$$

::: {.key-point}
These homogeneous directions form $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$; [Deck 06]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#homogeneous-systems-produce-subspaces)
develops the null space as a subspace
:::

::: {.notes}
[Deck 06]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#a-vector-space-starts-with-objects-and-two-operations) will verify the vector-space axioms and connect the null space to the
[row and column spaces]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#a-matrix-has-four-fundamental-subspaces).
:::

## Nonhomogeneous systems translate those directions {#nonhomogeneous-systems-translate-those-directions}

Suppose $\vct{x}_p$ is the coordinate column of one solution point of

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}
$$

Every solution has the form

$$
\vct{x}=\vct{x}_p+\vct{z},
\qquad
\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}
$$

Conversely, the difference between any two solutions is homogeneous:

$$
\mat{A}\vct{x}_1=\mat{A}\vct{x}_2=\vct{b}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mat{A}(\vct{x}_1-\vct{x}_2)=\vct{0}
$$

::: {.key-point}
For a consistent system, the solution set is an [affine set]{.alert}:<br>
Solution set $=$ one solution point $+$ all homogeneous directions
:::

## Free variables count the directions {#free-variables-count-the-directions}

For a consistent system with $n$ unknowns

| Free variables | Solution geometry |
|:---:|:---|
| $0$ | one point |
| $1$ | affine line |
| $2$ | affine plane |
| $k$ | $k$-parameter affine set |

If there are $r$ pivot variables, then there are

$$
n-r
$$

free variables

::: {.key-point}
The [dimension of the affine solution set]{.alert} is $n-r$, the number of free parameters<br>
It equals the dimension of the homogeneous direction space $\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a preview. Deck 06 will define
[basis]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#a-basis-balances-reach-and-economy) and
[dimension]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#dimension-counts-vectors-in-any-basis) and name the relationship
[rank–nullity]({{< meta decks.d06.file >}}#rank-nullity-counts-inputs).
:::

## Read the affine structure from elimination {#read-the-affine-structure-from-elimination}

Consider

\begin{align*}
x+y+z&=2\\
x-y+z&=0
\end{align*}

Elimination gives $y=1$ and $x+z=1$, hence

$$
\vct{x}
=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\\0\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{coordinates of one solution point}}
+t\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{homogeneous direction}}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Interpret this solution set
<span class="exsub">Verify that the direction satisfies $\mat{A}\vct{z}=\vct{0}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Explain why adding $t\vct{z}$ leaves both equations unchanged</span>
<span class="exsub">Decide whether the solution line passes through the origin</span>
</span>
:::

## Recall what the dot product already gives us {#recall-what-the-dot-product-already-gives-us}

[Deck 01 introduced the dot product]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#what-the-dot-product-reveals)
as the geometry on $\reals^n$

We now use only these consequences:

\begin{align*}
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=0
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\vct{u}\perp\vct{v}\\
\norm{\vct{v}}
&=\sqrt{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}\\
\operatorname{dist}(P,Q)
&=\norm{\vct{q}-\vct{p}}
\end{align*}

Notice the roles in the last line:

$$
\underbrace{Q-P}_{\text{vector}}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\norm{\vct{q}-\vct{p}}}_{\text{distance between points}}
$$

## Projection finds the nearest point on an affine line {#projection-finds-the-nearest-point-on-an-affine-line}

Let

$$
L=\{P+t\vct{v}:t\in\reals\},
\qquad \vct{v}\ne\vct{0}
$$

To compare another point $Q$ with $L$, first form the displacement

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vct{q}-\vct{p}
$$

Project that vector onto the line direction:

$$
\vct{p}_*
=\vct{p}
+\frac{(\vct{q}-\vct{p})^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}\vct{v}
$$

The result $\vct{p}_*$ gives coordinates of the point on $L$ nearest to $Q$

---

### Find the nearest point: a worked example {#nearest-point-worked-example}

$$
P=(1,1,0),\qquad \vct{v}=[1,0,1]^{\mathsf T},
\qquad Q=(4,2,1),\qquad L=\{P+t\vct{v}:t\in\reals\}
$$

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}
Use the [projection formula](#projection-finds-the-nearest-point-on-an-affine-line):

\begin{align*}
t_*&=\frac{(\vct{q}-\vct{p})^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}{\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}}
=\frac{4}{2}=2\\
\vct{p}_*&=\vct{p}+2\vct{v}=[3,1,2]^{\mathsf T}\\
\vct{q}-\vct{p}_*&=[1,1,-1]^{\mathsf T}
\end{align*}

Check: $(\vct{q}-\vct{p}_*)^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=1-1=0$
:::

::: {.column width="6%"}
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}

::: {.key-point}
Nearest point $P_*=(3,1,2)$; distance $\operatorname{dist}(Q,L)=\sqrt{3}$
:::

::: {.notes}
The residual is perpendicular to the line direction. For every $t$,
$\norm{\vct{q}-(\vct{p}+t\vct{v})}^2=3+2(t-2)^2$, so the minimum
occurs at $t=2$. Projecting $\vct{q}$ without first subtracting $\vct{p}$
would instead use the line through the origin and give the wrong answer.
:::

### Find the nearest point and distance {#nearest-point-exercise}

$$
P=(1,-1,0),\qquad \vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad Q=(4,0,2),\qquad L=\{P+t\vct{v}:t\in\reals\}
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Project a displacement to find the nearest point
<span class="exsub">Form $\vct{q}-\vct{p}$ and compute the minimizing parameter $t_*$</span>
<span class="exsub">Find the nearest point $P_*$ and the distance from $Q$ to $L$</span>
<span class="exsub">Verify that $\vct{q}-\vct{p}_*$ is perpendicular to $\vct{v}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Explain why projecting $\vct{q}$ onto $\vct{v}$ alone does not solve this problem</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The displacement is $(3,1,2)^{\mathsf T}$, so $t_*=5/5=1$.
The nearest point is $P_*=(2,1,0)$; the residual is $(2,-1,2)^{\mathsf T}$,
which has dot product zero with $(1,2,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and norm $3$.
The squared distance at parameter $t$ is $9+5(t-1)^2$.
Projecting $\vct{q}$ alone finds the nearest point on the parallel line through
the origin, not on the given affine line. Subtract the anchor point first,
project the displacement, then add the anchor point back.
:::

## A special 3D operation: the cross product {#the-cross-product-combines-two-directions}

For $\vct{u},\vct{v}\in\reals^3$, define

$$
\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
=\begin{bmatrix}
u_2v_3-u_3v_2\\
u_3v_1-u_1v_3\\
u_1v_2-u_2v_1
\end{bmatrix}
$$

The result is perpendicular to both inputs:

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})=0,
\qquad
\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})=0
$$

Its magnitude is parallelogram area, and reversing the inputs reverses its direction:

$$
\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}
=\norm{\vct{u}}\norm{\vct{v}}\sin\theta,
\qquad
\vct{v}\mathbin{\times}\vct{u}=-(\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v})
$$

The ordinary cross product is special to three-dimensional vectors

::: {.notes}
The natural generalization in other dimensions is the exterior, or wedge,
product. It records the oriented parallelogram determined by two vectors, but
its output is a bivector rather than another ordinary vector. In three
dimensions, perpendicularity identifies that oriented area with the vector
$\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}$. There is also an exceptional vector cross
product in dimension seven, but it is outside the scope of this course.
The wedge product belongs to exterior algebra, which generalizes oriented
areas, volumes, determinants, and the three-dimensional cross product.
:::

---

### A determinant pattern remembers the cross product {#a-determinant-pattern-remembers-the-cross-product}

Using the [standard basis vectors]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#standard-basis-vectors-reveal-every-column), remember

$$
\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
=\begin{vmatrix}
\vct{e}_1&\vct{e}_2&\vct{e}_3\\
u_1&u_2&u_3\\
v_1&v_2&v_3
\end{vmatrix}
$$

Expand across the first row with signs $+,-,+$:

\begin{align*}
\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
&=\vct{e}_1\begin{vmatrix}u_2&u_3\\v_2&v_3\end{vmatrix}
-\vct{e}_2\begin{vmatrix}u_1&u_3\\v_1&v_3\end{vmatrix}
+\vct{e}_3\begin{vmatrix}u_1&u_2\\v_1&v_2\end{vmatrix}
\end{align*}

Each $2\times2$ determinant uses $ad-bc$

::: {.key-point}
A [mnemonic, or memory aid]{.alert}, not a real determinant: the first row contains vectors
:::

---

### Why the cross-product norm is area {#why-the-cross-product-norm-is-area}

Squaring the [component formula](#the-cross-product-combines-two-directions) and collecting terms gives

\begin{align*}
\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}^2
&=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2)^2+(u_3v_1-u_1v_3)^2+(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)^2\\
&=(u_1^2+u_2^2+u_3^2)(v_1^2+v_2^2+v_3^2)
  -(u_1v_1+u_2v_2+u_3v_3)^2\\
&=\norm{\vct{u}}^2\norm{\vct{v}}^2-(\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v})^2
\end{align*}

For nonzero inputs, use the [dot-product cosine formula]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#what-the-dot-product-reveals):

$$
\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}^2
=\norm{\vct{u}}^2\norm{\vct{v}}^2(1-\cos^2\theta)
=\norm{\vct{u}}^2\norm{\vct{v}}^2\sin^2\theta
$$

::: {.key-point}
Parallelogram area $=$ base $\times$ perpendicular height
$=\norm{\vct{u}}\bigl(\norm{\vct{v}}\sin\theta\bigr)
=\norm{\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}}$
:::

If either vector is zero, both the area and the cross product are zero

::: {.notes}
The angle between nonzero vectors lies in $[0,\pi]$, so $\sin\theta\ge0$;
taking the nonnegative square root gives the stated norm. Parallel and
antiparallel inputs have zero height and area. In the algebraic identity,
the terms $u_i^2v_i^2$ cancel between the product of sums and the squared dot
product; the remaining square and mixed terms are exactly those obtained
by expanding the three cross-product components.
:::

---

### Compute a normal and an area {#compute-a-normal-and-an-area}

$$
\vct{u}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\vct{v}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\\3\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}
=\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot3-0\cdot1\\0\cdot0-1\cdot3\\1\cdot1-2\cdot0\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}6\\-3\\1\end{bmatrix}
=\vct{n}
$$

Check perpendicularity:

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}=6-6=0,
\qquad
\vct{v}^{\mathsf T}\vct{n}=-3+3=0
$$

::: {.key-point}
[Parallelogram area](#why-the-cross-product-norm-is-area) $=\norm{\vct{n}}=\sqrt{46}$; triangle area $=\sqrt{46}/2$
:::

## Point differences build a plane normal {#point-differences-build-a-plane-normal}

For three noncollinear points $P,Q,R\in\reals^3$, first form two directions:

$$
\vct{u}=\overrightarrow{PQ}=\vct{q}-\vct{p},
\qquad
\vct{v}=\overrightarrow{PR}=\vct{r}-\vct{p}
$$

Their cross product is a normal vector:

$$
\vct{n}=\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v},
\qquad
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{u}
=\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}\vct{v}=0
$$

The plane is therefore

$$
\vct{n}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{x}-\vct{p})=0
$$

---

### Find a plane and its triangle area {#find-a-plane-and-its-triangle-area}

$$
P=(1,0,1),\qquad Q=(2,1,1),\qquad R=(1,2,3)
$$

::: {.exitem .lettered}
<span class="exbullet">$\exstar$</span>
<span>Use point differences and a cross product
<span class="exsub">Find $\vct{u}=\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\vct{v}=\overrightarrow{PR}$</span>
<span class="exsub">Compute $\vct{n}=\vct{u}\mathbin{\times}\vct{v}$ and verify that it is perpendicular to both directions</span>
<span class="exsub">Find an equation for the affine plane through $P,Q,R$</span>
<span class="exsub">Find the area of triangle $PQR$; explain what changes if $Q$ and $R$ are exchanged</span>
</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
The directions are $(1,1,0)^{\mathsf T}$ and $(0,2,2)^{\mathsf T}$;
the cross product is $(2,-2,2)^{\mathsf T}$. Both dot products are zero.
The plane equation is $2(x-1)-2y+2(z-1)=0$, or $x-y+z=2$.
The triangle area is $\sqrt{3}$. Exchanging $Q$ and $R$ reverses the normal
but preserves the plane and the area.
:::

## The triple product reconnects to determinants {#the-triple-product-reconnects-to-determinants}

For vectors $\vct{u},\vct{v},\vct{w}\in\reals^3$,

$$
\vct{u}^{\mathsf T}(\vct{v}\mathbin{\times}\vct{w})
=\det\begin{bmatrix}\vct{u}&\vct{v}&\vct{w}\end{bmatrix}
$$

- absolute value — parallelepiped volume
- sign — orientation of the ordered directions
- zero — the directions lie in one plane

Point coordinates enter only through differences such as

$$
\overrightarrow{PQ},\quad
\overrightarrow{PR},\quad
\overrightarrow{PS}
$$

::: {.key-point}
Determinants measure the geometry of displacement vectors, independent of where the points are located
:::

# Big Ideas {data-state="goldborder"}

- Points are [locations]{.alert}; vectors are displacements or directions
- Choosing an origin lets both be represented by coordinate columns, but does not erase their different roles
- Homogeneous solutions form a vector space of directions through the origin
- A consistent nonhomogeneous solution set is one solution point plus all homogeneous directions
- The dot product tests orthogonality and measures point differences
- Cross products provide a special three-dimensional connection among point differences, normals, and determinants

# How Far We Have Come

[From matrix equations to the geometry of their solutions]{.alert}

- [Systems]({{< meta decks.d01.file >}}#read-the-solution-set) — elimination finds whether $\mat{A}\vct{x}=\vct{b}$ is consistent and where free directions remain
- [Matrix actions]({{< meta decks.d03.file >}}#geometry-of-matrix-transformations) — inverses undo reversible maps; determinants detect scale, orientation, and collapse
- [Points and directions]({{< meta decks.d05.file >}}#the-operations-reveal-the-roles) — subtract points to get vectors; add vectors to move points
- [Solution geometry]({{< meta decks.d05.file >}}#nonhomogeneous-systems-translate-those-directions) — every consistent solution set is $\vct{x}_p+\operatorname{Null}(\mat{A})$

::: {.key-point}
Solving now means describing [all solutions]{.alert}, not only finding one
:::
